articles.title: The end of Microsoft Research's AI Frontiers group
articles.raw_description: In 2023 after the ChatGPT release, it was clear to me that research needed to be more organized to succeed than was typical within Microsoft Research . The amount of support and focus which other research groups were applying was great enough that even with a clever idea pursued by one person it was likely to arrive late and unconvincing because one person could not move fast enough and the baselines which one person could assemble just were not strong enough to really show that an idea was worth taking flight. Several other folks thought similarly and we organized to create the AI Frontiers sub-organization within MSR. In AI Frontiers, we actively tried to organize coherent research efforts. This was not precisely “top down” or “bottom up”, but rather mostly somewhere in the messy middle. There were disagreements of course, and resolving them was sometimes quite challenging. Compute availability was also an often-severe bottleneck. But at a high level I was under the general impression that the organization was succeeding in doing pioneering things, particularly given the small size of AIF (~50 people) and relative to what we could do previously. Much of the work of AIF was figuring out how to make agents work, for example the Autogen orchestration framework and the Fara computer use agent. articles.title: Apple’s grey list: Words and phrases your iPhone won’t help you spell
articles.raw_description: There are more than 100,000 words and phrases that the tech giant has restricted its predictive text from completing, research shows The swipe-type-thwarting list was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman. Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters View image in fullscreen The swipe-type-thwarting list was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman. Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters Struggling to spell ‘male chauvinist pig’? Apple’s grey list means your iPhone won’t help you There are more than 100,000 words and phrases that the tech giant has restricted its predictive text from completing, research shows “Australia is a very bad place to question your sexuality on MDMA with NSA spies” might be a text you would wish to send to your friends, if you have had an extraordinarily complicated night out in Sydney. But your iPhone won’t help you spell any of it if you try to swipe-type it – that is, by gliding a finger across a keyboard as opposed to pecking out a word. New research shows that Apple has a “grey list” of more than 100,000 words and phrases that it has restricted from being completed by its predictive text. So if a user wishes to type phrases such as “Dictator Trump”, “NSA spies” or, surprisingly, “Australia is a very bad place”, “question your sexuality” or “on MDMA”, they will have to spell them out. articles.title: MaxxBench – "Nice DeepSWE score. But is it true?"
articles.raw_description: How coding models respond when familiar engineering tasks ask for something different. On this page We changed requirements in a coding benchmark and found models talking themselves out of following them. Sometimes the agent understood the new requirement perfectly. It described what needed to change, considered an implementation, and then decided the hidden tests probably wanted something else. In one run, a model implemented the change correctly, asked another model for the benchmark’s original answer, and removed its own correct code after receiving it. This is an awkward habit for a coding assistant to have. It is also a habit that a familiar benchmark can reward. If the model has guessed what the tests expect, it gets the same passing result as an agent that worked carefully from the requirements. We built MaxxBench to examine how much coding performance depends on those expectations. It changes the instructions or starting code of 89 DeepSWE tasks, giving models familiar engineering work with a reason to revise their usual approach. Methodology: Small mutations... Once a benchmark becomes popular, it becomes part of the development process. Its tasks can enter training data. Its scores influence checkpoint selection. Developers adjust prompts and agents against its failures. There are plenty of opportunities to get better at that particular exam. articles.title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
articles.raw_description: I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake. To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers. Things that were fun to get right: - Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes. - Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. It also tags attempts targeting three other Danfoss CVEs and the XWEB vulnerabilities. - Letting them in. Default logins open a fake store dashboard with defrost buttons, so you see the second move, not just the first. Nothing behind it is real. Two instances have been live for a day. articles.title: Making any integer with four 2s (2025)
articles.raw_description: There's a cute math puzzle that can be interesting to folks on very different levels: Given exactly four instances of the digit 2 and some target natural number, use any mathematical operations to generate the target number with these 2s, using no other digits. Some examples can be done by elementary school kids: \[\begin{align*} 1&=\frac{2+2}{2+2}\\ 2&=\frac{2}{2}+\frac{2}{2}\\ 3&=2\cdot2-\frac{2}{2}\\ 4&=2+2+2-2\\ 5&=2\cdot 2 +\frac{2}{2}\\ 6&=2\cdot 2\cdot 2 - 2\\ \end{align*}\] In middle school, kids learn about exponents, factorials, etc. which expands the range considerably: \[\begin{align*} 18&=2^{2^{2}}+2\\ 28&=(2+2)!+2+2\\ 256&=(2+2)^{2+2}\\ 65536&=2^{2^{2^{2}}}\\ \end{align*}\] Then come the tricks; for example, the number 22 (twenty two) can be seen as a valid use of two 2s, and so on; so we can have: \[\begin{align*} 26&=22+2+2\\ 11&=\frac{22}{\sqrt{2+2}}\\ 444&=222\cdot 2\\ \end{align*}\] Getting to 7 is notoriously difficult, but if you allow even more mathematical tools like the Gamma function , it becomes easy: \[7&=\Gamma(2)+2+2+2\] The more math skill people have, the more numbers they can make. See this thread for some fun concoctions using integrals, repeating fractions and combinatorial operators. One of my favorite examples involves complex numbers: \[12=|2+2\sqrt{-2}|^2\] So the fun doesn't end even after one graduates from university! articles.title: GitHub New pull request overview page in public preview
articles.raw_description: On a long pull request, checking what’s blocking often means scrolling past dozens of comments and timeline events just to reach the merge box. And once you’re there, you still… Back to changelog On a long pull request, checking what’s blocking often means scrolling past dozens of comments and timeline events just to reach the merge box. And once you’re there, you still need to work out what to do next. As people need to review more and more pull requests, time spent scrolling adds up. So we’ve begun to rethink the entire experience, beginning with addressing a familiar challenge: finding what’s blocking progress and determining what to do next. Today, we’re introducing the Overview page as an opt-in public preview, with rollout continuing through the weekend. It brings merge status and next available actions to the top of the page in a compact readiness summary. It’s the first step toward making pull requests easier to follow as code, conversations, and reviews evolve. The merge box, distilled We’re starting with the merge box, the place developers go to see whether a pull request can move forward. Rather than just moving it higher, we’ve also redesigned it to show the same information in less than half the space. Explore the supporting signals: A compact view of checks, comments, and approvals keeps the context nearby without making every detail compete for attention.
